h1: The Big Boat and the Rain
sub: A story from Genesis tells how a man named Noah built a big boat. Read the clues and put the story in order the way the text tells it.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: Your job is not to say if this story is true — your job is to notice what the story says and what happens first, next, and last. That is what good readers do.

win.h: You read the story like a detective!
win.p: You found what the text says and put it in the right order — without guessing. Great close reading!

clues.title: Where this story comes from
clues.body: This story is from the Book of Genesis, the first book of the Bible. We read it like any story — looking at who is in it, what happens, and what order things go in.

clues.title: Noah builds the ark
clues.body: In the story, God tells Noah to build a very big boat called an ark. Noah does what he is told and builds it.

clues.title: Animals come aboard
clues.body: After the ark is ready, animals come to Noah two by two — two of every kind. They all go onto the big boat.

clues.title: The rain comes down
clues.body: Then rain falls for a long time. Water covers the land. Noah, his family, and the animals are safe on the ark.

clues.title: Dry land at last
clues.body: When the rain stops, Noah sends out a dove. The dove comes back with a leaf, which means the water is going down. Soon dry land appears.

clues.title: True — but is it in this story?
clues.body: Blue whales are the biggest animals on Earth. They can grow as long as two school buses. That is a true and amazing fact — but it is not part of the Noah story.

locks.title: Put the flood story in order
locks.q: Tap the four parts in the order the Noah story tells them.
locks.reason: The text goes: build the ark, then animals come aboard, then rain and flood, then the dove finds dry land. Putting events in order is how readers follow what a story is really saying — clues 2, 3, 4, and 5 show it.

locks.title: Why did animals come on the ark?
locks.q: According to the story clues, animals came onto the ark…
options: Two by two, two of every kind
Only the big ones, like elephants
After the rain had already started
locks.reason: Clue 3 says animals came two by two, two of every kind, before the rain. Good readers answer from what the text says, not from a guess.

locks.title: Which facts are really in the Noah story?
locks.q: Check ONLY what the Noah story clues actually say. Leave out the true-but-off-topic one.

items.t: Noah built a big boat called an ark
Animals came onto the ark two by two
Blue whales can grow as long as two school buses
A dove helped Noah know the water went down

locks.reason: The blue whale fact is true but it is a decoy — it is not part of the Noah story. Strong readers spot when a fact is real but does not belong to the story being studied.

locks.title: Name the book
locks.q: Clue 1 tells you the name of the book this story comes from. Type its name.
locks.reason: Clue 1 says this story is from Genesis. Knowing where a text comes from helps us read it carefully and ask the right questions.

sub: A story from Luke tells about a hurt traveler and the people who walked by. Read the clues and find out who really helped.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: Your job is not to say if this story is true — your job is to notice what the text says about who helped and who did not. That is close reading.

win.p: You read the clues and answered from the text — not from a guess. That is exactly what good readers do.

clues.title: Where this story comes from
clues.body: This story is from the Book of Luke, in the Bible. A teacher tells it to show what it means to be a good neighbor. We read it like any story.

clues.title: A man gets hurt
clues.body: In the story, a man is walking on a road. Robbers attack him, take his things, and leave him hurt on the ground.

clues.title: Others walk past
clues.body: Two people see the hurt man and walk right past him. The story says they cross to the other side of the road. They do not stop.

clues.title: A stranger stops
clues.body: Then a man from another place — called a Samaritan — comes by. He stops, helps the hurt man, and takes care of him.

clues.title: What the helper does
clues.body: The Samaritan cleans the man's wounds, puts him on his own animal, takes him to a safe place, and pays for his care. The story shows what kindness looks like in action.

clues.title: True — but is it the point?
clues.body: Long ago, roads were often made of dirt or flat stones. Some Roman roads were so well built they lasted thousands of years. True — but that is not what this story is teaching.

locks.title: Who stopped to help the hurt man?
locks.q: According to the story clues, who stopped and helped the traveler?
options: A Samaritan, a man from another place
The first two people who saw him
A soldier who was passing by
locks.reason: Clue 4 says a Samaritan stopped and helped. Good readers answer from what the text says, not from what they already think.

locks.title: Put the story in order
locks.q: Tap the three parts in the order the Luke story tells them.

pads.e: 🚶 Man is hurt on the road

locks.reason: First the man is hurt, then two people pass by, then the Samaritan helps. Putting events in order shows us the cause and effect the story is teaching — clues 2, 3, and 4 show it.

locks.title: Which clues are really in the Good Samaritan story?
locks.q: Check ONLY what the story clues actually tell us. Leave out the true-but-off-topic one.

items.t: A man was left hurt on the road
Two people walked past without helping
Old Roman roads were made so well they lasted thousands of years
The Samaritan paid for the hurt man's care

locks.reason: The road-building fact is true but it is a decoy — it is not what this story is teaching. Separating relevant story details from interesting-but-off-topic facts is the key thinking move here.

locks.title: What did the helper show?
locks.q: Clue 5 says the story shows what one thing looks like in action, as the Samaritan cares for the hurt man. Type that one word from clue 5.
locks.reason: Clue 5 says the story shows what 'kindness' looks like in action. Finding the word a text uses to name a lesson is an important reading skill.

sub: A story from the Bible tells how a king named Solomon solved a very hard problem. Read the clues to find out how.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: Your job is to find out what the problem was, what the king did, and how it ended — just by reading the clues. No guessing needed!

win.h: You thought like a wise reader!
win.p: You followed the story step by step and answered only from the clues. That is great thinking.

clues.title: Where this story comes from
clues.body: This story is from the Bible, in a part called First Kings. King Solomon is known in the story for being very wise. We read it like any story.

clues.title: The hard problem
clues.body: Two women both say the same baby is theirs. Each woman says, 'That is my baby!' Solomon must figure out who is telling the truth.

clues.title: Solomon's surprising idea
clues.body: Solomon says, 'Bring me a sword. We will cut the baby in two and give half to each woman.' He does not really mean it — it is a test.

clues.title: A woman speaks up
clues.body: One woman cries out, 'No! Do not hurt the baby! Give the baby to her!' The other woman says go ahead and cut. Their answers are very different.

clues.title: The answer is clear
clues.body: Solomon says the woman who said 'do not hurt the baby' is the real mother — because a real mother wants her child to be safe and alive, even if it hurts her. He gives the baby to her.

clues.title: True — but is it the point?
clues.body: Gold is one of the heaviest metals on Earth. A single gold bar used in banks weighs about 27 pounds. True and interesting — but not what this story is teaching.

locks.title: What was the hard problem?
locks.q: According to the story clues, what problem did Solomon need to solve?
options: Two women both claimed the same baby was theirs
A baby was lost in the king's palace
Two kings were fighting over a city
locks.reason: Clue 2 says two women both claimed the same baby. Good readers find the problem in the text — they do not guess or add details the text does not give.

locks.title: Put the story in order
locks.q: Tap the three parts in the order the story tells them.
locks.reason: First comes the problem (two women, one baby), then the king's test with the sword, then the answer is revealed. Reading in order helps us see how a wise character solves a problem — clues 2, 3, and 5 show it.

locks.title: Which clues are really in the Solomon story?
locks.q: Check ONLY what the story clues actually tell us. Leave out the true-but-off-topic one.

items.t: Two women both said the same baby was theirs
Solomon used a surprising test to find the truth
A gold bar used in banks weighs about 27 pounds
The real mother said do not hurt the baby

locks.reason: The gold bar fact is true but is a decoy — it has nothing to do with this story. Spotting the true-but-off-topic clue is a key critical thinking skill.

locks.title: What is Solomon known for?
locks.q: Clue 1 tells us what King Solomon is known for in this story. Type that one word.
locks.reason: Clue 1 says Solomon is known for being 'wise.' Naming a character's trait from the text — not from what you already know — is close reading.

h1: The Man and the Big Fish
sub: A story from the Book of Jonah tells what happened when a man tried to run away from a job he was given. Read the clues and put it in order.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: This story has a lot of steps. Your job is to find the right order, answer only from the clues, and spot the fact that does not belong.

win.p: You put the story in order and answered from the text. That is exactly what close readers do.

clues.title: Where this story comes from
clues.body: This story is from the Book of Jonah, in the Bible. It is a short book with a big adventure. We read it like any story — noticing what happens and in what order.

clues.title: Jonah gets a job — and runs
clues.body: In the story, Jonah is told to go to a big city called Nineveh. Instead of going, he gets on a boat and sails the other way.

clues.title: A storm shakes the boat
clues.body: A huge storm hits the sea. The sailors are scared. Jonah tells them he is running away and that the storm is because of him. He asks them to throw him into the sea.

clues.title: A great fish swallows Jonah
clues.body: A great fish swallows Jonah whole. The story says Jonah is inside the fish for three days and three nights.

clues.title: Jonah comes out — and goes
clues.body: After three days, the fish puts Jonah back on dry land. This time, Jonah goes to the city of Nineveh, just as he was told.

clues.title: True — but is it in the story?
clues.body: Great white sharks can smell a tiny drop of blood from far away. They are amazing hunters. That is a true fact about sharks — but it is not part of the Jonah story.

locks.title: Put Jonah's story in order
locks.q: Tap the four parts in the order the Book of Jonah tells them.
locks.reason: The story goes: Jonah runs the wrong way, then a storm hits, then a fish swallows him, then after three days he goes to the city. Putting events in the right order is how we follow what a story is really showing — clues 2, 3, 4, and 5 show it.

locks.title: How long was Jonah inside the fish?
locks.q: According to Clue 4, how long did Jonah stay inside the great fish?
locks.reason: Clue 4 says three days and three nights. Answering from the exact words of the text — not guessing — is the key reading skill here.

locks.title: Which clues are really in the Jonah story?
locks.q: Check ONLY what the story clues actually tell us. Leave out the true-but-off-topic one.

items.t: Jonah sailed the wrong way instead of going to Nineveh
A great fish swallowed Jonah for three days
Great white sharks can smell blood from far away
After the fish, Jonah went to the city as he was told

locks.reason: The shark fact is true but it is a decoy — sharks do not appear in the Jonah story. Strong readers notice when a fact is real but off topic.

locks.title: Name the book
locks.q: Clue 1 names the book this story comes from. Type its name.
locks.reason: Clue 1 says this story is from the Book of Jonah. Knowing the source of a text is the first step in reading it carefully.

sub: A story from Exodus tells how Moses came down from a mountain with ten rules. Read the clues and count along.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: Your job is to find what the text says about the rules, where they come from, and what book tells the story — just by reading the clues. Ready? Let's go!

win.p: You found the answers in the clues and named the source. That is exactly what good readers do.

clues.title: Where this story comes from
clues.body: This story is from the Book of Exodus, in the Bible. Exodus is a long story about a man named Moses and a people trying to get to a new home.

clues.title: Moses goes up
clues.body: In the story, Moses goes up a tall mountain. The story says God speaks to him there and gives him ten rules for how to live together.

clues.title: Rules written in stone
clues.body: The ten rules are written on two flat pieces of stone. People often call them the Ten Commandments. There are exactly ten — not nine, not eleven.

clues.title: Rules to live by
clues.body: Some of the rules are about how to treat other people — do not steal, do not lie, respect your parents. The story says these rules help people live well together.

clues.title: The people were waiting
clues.body: While Moses was on the mountain, all the people waited at the bottom. They had been traveling for a long time through a desert to find their new home.

clues.title: True — but is it the point?
clues.body: The tallest mountain in the world is Mount Everest. It is so tall that the air at the top is very thin. True and amazing — but that is not what this story is teaching.

locks.title: How many rules did Moses bring?
locks.q: According to the story clues, how many rules did Moses carry down the mountain?
locks.reason: Clue 3 says there are exactly ten rules — the Ten Commandments. Reading carefully for exact numbers is an important close-reading skill.

locks.title: Put the story in order
locks.q: Tap the three parts in the order the Exodus story tells them.
locks.reason: Moses goes up the mountain first, then receives the ten rules, then the story tells what those rules are for. Reading in order shows us how the story builds — clues 2, 3, and 4 show it.

locks.title: Which clues are really in the Moses story?
locks.q: Check ONLY what the story clues actually tell us. Leave out the true-but-off-topic one.

items.t: Moses went up a mountain and received ten rules
The rules were written on two flat pieces of stone
Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world
Some rules say do not steal and respect your parents

locks.reason: The Mount Everest fact is true but it is a decoy — it has nothing to do with the Moses story. Telling the difference between story evidence and a true-but-off-topic fact is the heart of this thinking move.

locks.title: Name the book
locks.q: Clue 1 names the book this Moses story comes from. Type its name.
locks.reason: Clue 1 says this story is from the Book of Exodus. Naming the source of a text is the first thing a careful reader does.
